script.opening: “My periods are all over the place, I’m not sleeping, I’m drenched at night and I can’t think straight. Is this the change? Do I need a blood test to find out?”

facts.text: A year of irregular cycles (3 to 8 weeks). Last period 7 weeks ago. Hot flushes several times a day, worse in uniform; night sweats most nights; waking at 3am. Irritable, aching joints, low libido, vaginal dryness. No postcoital or intermenstrual bleeding.
Condoms most of the time with her partner of three years. Could she be pregnant? “Surely not at 46.” Willing to do a test. Does not want a pregnancy.
Non-smoker. No migraine. No clots in her or her family. No breast cancer in the family. Mother had dementia from 68. Last cervical screening up to date.

facts.topic: Only if asked about the brain fog and work
facts.text: Losing words, walking into rooms and forgetting why. Two paperwork errors at work led to an informal performance review. Frightened: “Mum started like this.” Hasn’t told work about menopause symptoms.
Low and tearful at times, more irritable; still enjoys walking the dog and her nieces. Sleep poor. No thoughts of self-harm. Alcohol: a glass of wine most nights “to sleep”.
Wants to know what this is and to feel normal. Open to HRT; assumed it would “cover contraception too”. Worried about breast cancer “a bit”. Would consider a coil.

Brisk and organised, uses humour. Becomes quiet and tearful when the brain fog and her mother come up. Relieved when the cognitive symptoms are explained and taken seriously, and when the doctor offers to help with work.

ice.ideas: “It’s probably the change, but I need a blood test to prove it.”
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA: fear of early dementia like her mother, and of losing her job after a performance review. Also a belief that HRT will act as contraception.
ice.expectations: “A blood test, and HRT if it’s the menopause.”

checkpoints.text: Takes a menstrual and symptom history and makes a clinical diagnosis of perimenopause without FSH testing (NICE NG23: over 45 with symptoms), checking for red-flag bleeding
Excludes pregnancy (late period, inconsistent condom use) and asks about contraception
Explores the cognitive symptoms, uncovers the fear of dementia and the work review, screens mood and alcohol, and explains that brain fog is common in perimenopause, to be reviewed after treatment
Explains HRT options: oestrogen with a progestogen for endometrial protection because she has a uterus; transdermal or oral oestrogen; vaginal oestrogen for genitourinary symptoms

Explains that HRT is not contraception and offers the 52 mg LNG-IUS as both the progestogen part of HRT and contraception (check the SPC), or other suitable contraception, continued until no longer needed (CoSRH: until 55, or 2 years’ amenorrhoea if under 50)
Mentions CBT for vasomotor and mood symptoms and non-hormonal options, and gives proportionate, honest risk information
Supports work: discusses telling her manager, reasonable adjustments, occupational health referral and a fit note with adjustments if helpful
Uses shared decision-making, checks understanding and arranges review (bleeding pattern, symptom response, cognitive symptoms) with a safety-net for abnormal bleeding

worked.txt: “At 46, with irregular periods, flushes and night sweats, this is very likely the perimenopause. The guidance says we don’t need a blood test to diagnose it, because hormone levels jump around and a single test can mislead.”
“Your last period was seven weeks ago and condoms aren’t always used, so let’s do a pregnancy test before we start anything.”
“You said you can’t think straight. What worries you most about that?”
“Losing words and forgetting tasks is really common in the perimenopause, especially with broken sleep. It usually improves with treatment. If it doesn’t, we’ll look into it properly, I promise.”
“HRT doesn’t stop you getting pregnant. A hormonal coil can do two jobs: it protects the womb lining as part of HRT and gives contraception. Then you’d add oestrogen as a patch or gel.”
“Would it help to tell your manager it’s menopause? Occupational health can suggest adjustments, like uniform, breaks or ventilation, and I can write a fit note with suggestions if useful.”

f.learning: NICE NG23 (Menopause: identification and management, updated 2024) advises diagnosing perimenopause clinically in women over 45 with vasomotor symptoms and irregular periods, without FSH testing. Exclude pregnancy where periods are late and contraception is inconsistent. HRT for a woman with a uterus needs oestrogen plus a progestogen for endometrial protection; transdermal oestrogen does not increase VTE risk above baseline and suits women with risk factors. HRT is not contraception. The 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine system can provide both the progestogen component of HRT and contraception (check the SPC for licensed duration of use for each purpose). CoSRH guidance on contraception for women over 40 advises continuing contraception until age 55, or stopping after 2 years of amenorrhoea if under 50 (1 year if over 50) when not using hormonal methods. NG23 also recommends offering CBT as an option for vasomotor symptoms and for low mood associated with menopause, and vaginal oestrogen for genitourinary symptoms. Cognitive complaints (“brain fog”) are common in perimenopause and often improve with treatment of vasomotor symptoms and sleep; screen mood and alcohol, and reassess if symptoms persist, especially with a family history of dementia. Work matters: many women do not disclose menopause symptoms at work; occupational health, reasonable adjustments and a fit note with suggested adaptations can help. Risk communication should be balanced and proportionate; for women in their 40s the absolute risks of HRT are small. The hidden agenda here is fear of inherited dementia and of losing her job.

model.text: Hello Nicola, I’m Dr Clarke. What’s been happening?
My periods are all over the place, I’m not sleeping, I’m drenched at night and I can’t think straight. Is this the change? Do I need a blood test to find out?
Let’s find out. Tell me about your periods over the last year, and when the last one was.
Anything from three to eight weeks apart. Last one seven weeks ago. Hot flushes all day, especially in uniform.
Any bleeding between periods or after sex, or very heavy bleeding?
No.
What are you using for contraception, and is there any chance you could be pregnant?
Condoms, most of the time. Surely not at 46? I’ll do a test.
Any migraines, clots in you or the family, breast cancer in the family? Do you smoke?
None of those. Never smoked.
You said you can’t think straight. What worries you most about that?
(pause, tearful) I’ve made mistakes at work. I’m on a performance review. My mum got dementia at 68 and it started like this. I’m terrified.
That’s a frightening thing to carry, especially after your mum. Thank you for telling me. How has your mood been, and how much are you drinking to help you sleep?
Low sometimes, irritable. Still enjoy walking the dog. A glass of wine most nights. Nothing darker than that.

At 46, with irregular periods, flushes and night sweats, this is very likely the perimenopause. We don’t need a blood test to diagnose it, because hormone levels swing around and one test can mislead. Losing words and forgetting tasks is really common in the perimenopause, especially with broken sleep, and usually improves with treatment. If it doesn’t, we’ll look into it properly.
model.why: Clinical diagnosis; brain fog explained with a plan

model.text: So it’s not the start of what Mum had?
Nothing you’ve told me points that way, and the timing fits the hormones. I’ll review it with you once you’re sleeping better.

HRT is a good option. Because you have a womb, you need oestrogen plus a progestogen to protect the lining. One important point: HRT isn’t contraception. A hormonal coil could do two jobs, protecting the womb lining and giving contraception, with oestrogen as a patch or gel. Patches and gels don’t raise the clot risk.
I assumed HRT would cover contraception. A coil sounds sensible.

You’d need contraception until 55, or until two years without a period if that happens before 50. There’s also a type of talking therapy, CBT, that helps flushes, sleep and mood, which you could do alongside. The risks of HRT at your age are small, and I can go through them in numbers before you decide.
And work: would it help to tell your manager this is the menopause? Occupational health can suggest adjustments, and I can write a fit note with suggestions if useful.
Can you tell me what we’ve agreed?
Pregnancy test today. Coil plus a patch or gel. Not contraception on its own. CBT. Talk to my inspector and occupational health. Review the brain fog.
Exactly. I’ll see you three months after starting. If you have bleeding after sex, between periods, or very heavy bleeding, tell me sooner.

social.t: Many women hide symptoms at work, especially in uniformed or male-dominated roles. Errors are sometimes treated as performance issues.
A parent’s dementia makes cognitive symptoms frightening. Ask about it.

legal.t: Menopause-related treatment at work may engage protections for sex, age or disability. Employers are encouraged to make reasonable adjustments.
A fit note can state “may be fit for work” with suggested adjustments (DWP guidance).

professional.t: Present options with balanced, proportionate risk information (GMC Decision making and consent).
Avoid unnecessary FSH testing; it can mislead in the perimenopause.

community.t: Can advise employer and employee on adjustments and support.
NHS menopause information, British Menopause Society/Women’s Health Concern patient resources.

items.fix: Explain and offer the LNG-IUS or other method.

wordPics.fail: Orders FSH; starts HRT without excluding pregnancy or mentioning contraception; ignores the brain fog or dismisses it; never discovers the work review or her mother’s dementia.
wordPics.pass: Diagnoses perimenopause clinically, excludes pregnancy, explains HRT is not contraception and offers suitable options, and addresses the brain fog.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: uncovers the dementia fear and work review with empathy; proportionate reassurance with a review plan; offers the LNG-IUS for both roles and transdermal oestrogen; CBT; practical work support; clear safety-net.

avoid.dont: “Let’s check your FSH to confirm it.”
avoid.instead: “At 46 with these symptoms we can diagnose it without a blood test.”
avoid.why: NICE NG23 advises against FSH testing in women over 45 with typical symptoms.

avoid.instead: “HRT isn’t contraception. A hormonal coil can protect your womb and prevent pregnancy.”
avoid.why: Unplanned pregnancy risk in the perimenopause.

avoid.dont: “Brain fog is just the menopause, don’t worry.”
avoid.instead: “It’s very common now and usually improves; we’ll review it and look further if not.”
avoid.why: Dismissing it ignores her fear and the need to reassess.
